title: The Complete 10-Tetrahedra Census of Orientable Cusped Hyperbolic 3-Manifolds
abstract: We extend the complete census of orientable cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds to 10 tetrahedra, giving the next 150,730 manifolds and their 496,638 minimal ideal triangulations. As applications, we find the precisely 439,898 exceptional Dehn fillings on them, revealing the next 1,849 simplest hyperbolic knot exteriors in S³. We also give the simplest example of an orientable cusped hyperbolic 3-manifold containing a closed totally geodesic surface.

      Abstract
We extend the complete census of orientable cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds to 10 tetrahedra, giving
the next 150,730 manifolds and their 496,638 minimal ideal triangulations. As applications, we find
the precisely 439,898 exceptional Dehn fillings on them, revealing the next 1,849 simplest hyperbolic
knot exteriors in S 3 . We also give the simplest example of an orientable cusped hyperbolic 3-manifold
containing a closed totally geodesic surface.

 1      Introduction
The enumeration of examples has been of fundamental importance in the study of low-
dimensional topology ever since Tait gave the first knot table in 1884 [41]. The censuses of
knots have been extensively explored over the years, all the way to approximately the first 2
billion knots [28, 8, 43]. However, the censuses of orientable cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds,
initiated by Hildebrand and Weeks [25], have seen no progress after the 44,250 manifolds
whose minimal ideal triangulations consist of 9 tetrahedra were given by Burton in 2014 [7].
In this paper, we extend the census by giving the 150,730 manifolds whose minimal ideal
triangulations consist of 10 tetrahedra. Table 1 summarizes the timeline of the development
of censuses of orientable cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds.
    By hyperbolic 3-manifolds, we mean 3-manifolds with Riemannian metrics of constant
curvature −1 that are complete as metric spaces; in particular their geodesics can be extended
indefinitely in length. A hyperbolic 3-manifold is cusped if it has a topological end that is of
finite volume. An orientable cusped finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifold is homeomorphic
to the interior of a compact 3-manifold whose boundary is a non-empty union of tori. Our
main result is the following:
▶ Theorem 1. There are precisely 150,730 orientable cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds whose
minimal ideal triangulations consist of 10 tetrahedra. Moreover, there are precisely a total of
496,638 minimal ideal triangulations of these manifolds.

           We highlight here that in order to obtain Theorem 1, we applied a new core technique,
       the verified canonical triangulations. We anticipate that a mixture of this technique with
       traditional ones would suffice for further extension of the census, provided successful generation
       of the candidates; see Sections 3.1 and 3.5 for more detailed discussions.
           Throughout this paper, we assume triangulations consist of finitely many tetrahedra. If
       a cusped hyperbolic 3-manifold admits an ideal triangulation, each tetrahedron has finite
       volume [15, §2.5], hence the volume of the manifold is finite. Conversely, any cusped
       finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifold has an ideal triangulation given by a refinement of the
       Epstein–Penner cellulation [37, §5]. Therefore, for cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds, being finite-
       volume is equivalent to admitting ideal triangulations, hence we drop the term finite-volume
       when talking about cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds admitting ideal triangulations.
           In general, it is unknown whether all cusped finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifolds admit
       geometric triangulations in the sense of Section 2.1 below [36]. However, when certifying
       hyperbolicity, SnapPy returns true if and only if it finds a geometric triangulation. Therefore
       an immediate corollary of this paper is that
       ▶ Corollary 2. All cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds ideally triangulable by at most 10 tetrahedra
       admit geometric triangulations.
       Note that nonorientable manifolds are included here since they are included in Theorem 7.
       For orientable manifolds, the above result can be strengthened to Proposition 11.
           We briefly review the needed terminologies in Section 2, then give detailed discussions in
       Section 3 for the creation of the 10-tetrahedra census, after which we give some applications
       of the extended census in Section 4. All corresponding code and data are available at [34].

        2      Preliminaries
       2.1     Triangulations
       A (generalised) triangulation T is a disjoint union of finitely many tetrahedra, with some or
       all faces identified in pairs via simplicial maps, and we avoid identifications where an edge
       is identified with itself in reverse. Note that T is not necessarily a simplicial complex, as
       identifications of two faces of the same tetrahedron are allowed.
           Quotienting by the identifications, T can be seen as a topological space, along with
       a cellular structure induced by the tetrahedra. A vertex in T is a 0-cell in this cellular
       structure, and an edge is a 1-cell. The link of a vertex in T is the frontier of a small regular
       neighborhood of that vertex. A vertex is internal if its link is a sphere, and is ideal if its link
       is some other closed surface. For an edge e in T , its degree is the cardinality of the set

▶ Definition 3. Let M be the interior of a compact 3-manifold with boundary. A triangulation
T is an ideal triangulation of M if it is homeomorphic to M after removing its ideal vertices,
and is minimal if no ideal triangulation of M with fewer tetrahedra exists.

It follows that every vertex of an ideal triangulation is either internal or ideal. Note that an
ideal triangulation itself is not a manifold and has at least one ideal vertex.
    If M is a cusped hyperbolic 3-manifold, an ideal triangulation T of M is geometric if all
vertices are ideal, all edges are geodesics, all 2-cells are parts of geodesic planes, and no flat
or negatively oriented tetrahedron (i.e. with zero or negative volume) exists.
    The following results were proven in Section 3 of [7]:

▶ Lemma 4 (Burton). Let T be a minimal ideal triangulation of a cusped hyperbolic 3-
manifold. Then T contains no internal vertices.

▶ Lemma 5 (Burton). Let T be a minimal ideal triangulation of a cusped hyperbolic 3-
manifold. Then T has no edges of degree 1 or 2, and T has no edges of degree 3 that are
contained in three distinct tetrahedra.

2.2    Normal surfaces
In a tetrahedron, an arc α properly embedded in one of its faces is normal if the endpoints of
α are in the interior of distinct edges. A properly embedded disk is a triangle if its boundary
consists of three normal arcs in distinct faces, and is a square if its boundary consists of four
normal arcs in distinct faces.
    Let T be a triangulation. A properly embedded compact surface in T is normal if its
intersection with every tetrahedron in T (with the identifications undone) is a properly
embedded surface whose connected components consist of only triangles and squares.
    An isotopy of T is normal if it preserves the cellular structure of T . Up to normal isotopy,
there are 4 triangles and 3 squares in a tetrahedron. Multiple copies of triangles or squares
in the same normal isotopy class may appear in the intersection of a normal surface and a
tetrahedron. It follows that a normal surface in a triangulation of n tetrahedra is uniquely
determined by a vector in N7n up to normal isotopy, where N := {k ∈ Z | k ≥ 0}.
    The subset N := {v ∈ N7n | v represents a normal surface} consists of integral vectors
in a certain non-convex subset of a polyhedral cone in R7n [29]. The standard vertex normal
surfaces correspond to vertices of a cross-section of this polyhedral cone, and can be viewed
as forming a finite basis for N .
    The following result was proven in Section 3 of [7]:

▶ Lemma 6 (Burton). Let T be a minimal ideal triangulation of a cusped hyperbolic 3-
manifold. Then no standard vertex normal surface in T
  has positive Euler characteristic; or
  has zero Euler characteristic, is not a vertex link, and in addition
     is one-sided; or
     is two-sided, and if we cut T open along it then no component of the resulting space is
     a solid torus or solid Klein bottle.

        3     Creating the 10-tetrahedra census

       3.1    Overview
       To build a census (of knots, manifolds, etc), the procedure generally follows a 3-step outline:
          (i) Generate all candidates for the census.
         (ii) Decide the eligibility of each candidate.
        (iii) Group eligible candidates into isomorphism classes and certify that the isomorphism
              classes are all distinct.
       As long as the candidate generation is performed exhaustively and the eligibility for each
       candidate is decided correctly, the census obtained is guaranteed to contain all wanted objects.
       With step (iii), the resulting census will contain no duplicates. We say that a census is
       complete if it contains all wanted objects without any duplicated ones.
            For censuses of cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds, the candidates will be ideal triangulations
       consisting of a given number of tetrahedra, and the eligibility conditions will be minimality (of
       triangulations) and hyperbolicity (of manifolds the triangulations represent). For certifying
       distinctness, algebraic invariants were widely applied for both the census of hyperbolic
       3-manifolds [7] and the census of knots [28, 8, 43]. However, it is unknown whether algebraic
       methods will indeed separate all given isometry classes within a given scope, consequently
       they cannot be used to certify if two isometry classes are indeed the same, and other methods
       will be required for that purpose. Here we propose an alternative approach for cusped
       hyperbolic 3-manifolds, using a geometric invariant, the canonical triangulation, built upon
       the Epstein–Penner canonical cellulation [21] by Weeks [44], whose rigorous computation
       was implemented by Goerner [24]. An introduction to these can be found in [22], and we
       review them briefly in Section 3.3.1. The canonical triangulation, when computed rigorously,
       is a complete invariant of cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds, and we applied it to deduplicate a
       majority of triangulations in the 10-tetrahedra census in Section 3.3.3.
            Our approaches for steps (i) and (ii) largely overlap with those in [7]. For completeness,
       we briefly describe them in Section 3.2, and kindly refer the reader to [7] for more details.
       For step (iii), detailed discussions will be given in Section 3.3.

    With the candidates generated, we proceed to determine their eligibilities. For an ideal
triangulation to remain in the census, it must be both minimal and representing a cusped
hyperbolic 3-manifold. Hence an ideal triangulation is discarded immediately if it is certified
to be nonminimal or representing a non-hyperbolic 3-manifold. If an ideal triangulation is
certified to represent a cusped hyperbolic 3-manifold, we temporarily keep it, and decide
whether it is minimal by checking if it represents a manifold that has already appeared in
censuses with fewer tetrahedra, which we discuss in Section 3.3.
    Four tests were used in Table 2, which we describe below:
Greedy nonminimality: we use Regina’s highly efficient simplification algorithm [5] to try
    converting each candidate into an ideal triangulation with fewer tetrahedra, while repre-
    senting the same 3-manifold. If such a triangulation with fewer tetrahedra is found, then
    the candidate is nonminimal.
Exhaustive nonminimality: given an integer parameter h > 0, for each candidate with n
    tetrahedra (n = 10 in our settings), enumerate all triangulations that can be reached via
    2-3 and 3-2 Pachner moves without ever exceeding n + h tetrahedra. If a triangulation
    with fewer than n tetrahedra is found during the process, the candidate is nonminimal.
Special surfaces: for each candidate T , enumerate all standard vertex normal surfaces in it,
    and check if any of them
       has positive Euler characteristic; or
       has zero Euler characteristic, is not a vertex link, and in addition
          is one-sided; or
          is two-sided, and if we cut T open along it then no component of the resulting space
          is a solid torus or solid Klein bottle.
    If any such surface is found, then by Lemma 6, T is either nonminimal or does not
    represent a cusped hyperbolic 3-manifold.
Certify hyperbolicity: given an integer parameter r > 0, for each candidate T , we randomize
    it by doing random Pachner moves, and ask SnapPy to try finding a complete hyperbolic
    structure on T , which uses an algorithm similar to HIKMOT’s [27], where affirmative
    answers are rigorous [24]. If the answer is not affirmative, we randomize T and try again,
    until an affirmative answer is achieved or the number of attempts reaches r.
We summarize the tests along with their core functions in Table 4 in [33, Appendix A.1].

       3.3     Grouping and Separating
       In this section, we discuss the procedure for step (iii) described in Section 3.1. A central
       tool for it, in both [7] and our method, is the canonical triangulation of cusped finite-volume
       hyperbolic 3-manifolds.

           The Epstein–Penner cellulation is invariant under the choice of the volume of cusp

              for each vertex u originally in e, add an edge connecting v and u;

              the vertex added to the interior of e2 .

       ▶ Definition 9. The canonical triangulation of M is the Epstein–Penner cellulation of M if
       the latter is a triangulation, and the subdivision of the Epstein–Penner cellulation described
       above otherwise.

          Weeks established a heuristic procedure which, given a geometric triangulation, computes
       the Epstein–Penner cellulation of the corresponding cusped hyperbolic 3-manifold via local
       modifications, doing 2-3 and 3-2 Pachner moves wherever tetrahedra meet concavely at
       faces or edges [44]. The canonical triangulation can then be easily computed from the
       Epstein–Penner cellulation. The methods for both were implemented in SnapPea in the
       1990s, and later inherited by its successor SnapPy [13]. In their original implementations,
       the hyperbolic structures used were only recorded numerically, hence accuracy issues may
       come into play, which we discuss in the following two sections.

3.3.2      Burton’s method: algebraic certification
Let us briefly review the method Burton used in [7], which can be summarized as:
1. For each ideal triangulation, compute its canonical triangulation numerically using
    SnapPea, and partition them into classes by the canonical triangulations computed.
2. For triangulations in each class, perform an exhaustive search through 2-3 and 3-2 Pachner
    moves, attempting to identify classes that should have been merged in step 1, but were
    not due to numerical accuracy issues, thus refining the partitioning.
3. For each class, compute the list {orientability, H1 = π1ab , S2ab (π1 ), . . . , Skab (π1 )} of alge-
    braic invariants to certify that all groups are distinct, increasing k if necessary, where
    Siab (G) is the multi-set of abelianisations of index i subgroups of G, one subgroup for
    each conjugacy class. For the 9-tetrahedra census, k = 11 was required and sufficed.
Note that to confirm the completeness of previous censuses, Burton dealt with all candidates
with no more than 9 tetrahedra at once, hence triangulations that were grouped with
triangulations with fewer tetrahedra were discarded immediately due to nonminimality.
    There are several aspects where numerical computation could cause issues in step 1:
    A quantity tilt is used to characterize whether tetrahedra meet concavely, parallelly or
    convexly, each corresponding to the tilt being positive, zero, or negative respectively [44,
    40]. When the absolute value of tilt is small, the numerical computation may falsely
    recognize the sign of tilt, resulting in an incorrect canonical triangulation.
    Flat tetrahedra being falsely recognized as non-flat, which would then be incorrectly dealt
    with when subdividing Epstein–Penner triangulations into canonical triangulations.

    When the above issues arise in step 1, SnapPea/SnapPy fails to find the correct canonical
triangulation and arrives at an incorrect one, while still representing the same manifold
as the input triangulation. Hence steps 2 and 3 were necessary to spot and resolve these
miscomputed cases. However, steps 2 and 3 can be very expensive to perform, and require
back-and-forth adjustments of parameters. Furthermore, although successful for censuses
with at most 9 tetrahedra, it is unknown whether step 3 will separate all cases within a
computable scope, or even if it will separate all of them in theory [23].
▶ Remark 10. We remark here that the subdividing algorithm Weeks implemented in
SnapPea/SnapPy does not work for refinements of Epstein–Penner cellulations containing flat
tetrahedra. This led to the miscomputed example x101 found by Burton [6] and mentioned

During the course of this project, the author found another such example, o9_43806 and
located the said cause. This bug has been fixed in SnapPy 3.3 by forcing it to find a

3.3.3      Our method: verified computation
Instead of making up for the mistakes caused by numerical computation of canonical
triangulations using other methods, we enhance the computation itself to avoid the mistakes
directly. With the accuracy issues described in the previous section, this requires us to:
(a) given two supposedly different quantities, rigorously tell which one is larger;
(b) given two supposedly equal quantities, prove that they are equal.

           For (a), we use interval arithmetics, which can be thought of as computation with
       controlled errors. If two quantities are different, with sufficiently small error the lower bound
       of one will be strictly larger than the upper bound of another, revealing the larger quantity.
       Similar approach was also used in HIKMOT’s rigorous certification of hyperbolicity [27].
           For (b), we use the LLL algorithm [32] to symbolically solve the trace field of hyperbolic
       structure, representing it as a number field. We then express the quantities as elements in
       the number field, hence they are equal if and only if their difference is the zero element.
           The above enhanced computation was implemented in SnapPy by M. Goerner [24], and is
       called verified computation. We refer the reader to [20, 22] for more detailed discussions.
           Canonical triangulations obtained with verified computation are thus provably correct.
       Let us call a supposedly canonical triangulation obtained by SnapPy a verified canonical
       triangulation if it was obtained with verified computation, and an unverified canonical
       triangulation if the computation was performed purely numerically.

            In particular, cu is injective. The verified canonical triangulation is then a branch of
       cu , a single-valued function cv : {M} → {T }. Since cu is injective, cv is also injective,

           Although the definition of canonical triangulation does not require the manifold to be
       orientable, the current implementation of verified computation for canonical triangulations
       in SnapPy does not work for nonorientable ones with multiple cusps. Hence we discard the
       nonorientable candidates and deal with the remaining 608,918 orientable ones.
           We successfully computed the verified canonical triangulations for all except 16 of the
       608,918 orientable candidates. The 16 cases failed due to their trace fields being too
       complicated; we remark that this very nature intrinsically separates them from the others,
       though further investigation is still required to prove it. By comparing the results with the
       verified canonical triangulations of all manifolds in censuses of at most 9 tetrahedra, we
       obtained 496,622 minimal triangulations of 10 tetrahedra, which, grouped by their verified
       canonical triangulations, give 150,724 distinct manifolds. For the 16 candidates whose
       verified canonical triangulations were not computed, we computed the first 60 digits of their
       hyperbolic volumes using interval arithmetics [24] and their first homology groups, which
       separated them from all manifolds in censuses up to 9 tetrahedra plus the 150,724 ones,
       and grouped them into 6 classes; within each class, the triangulations were confirmed to all
       represent the same manifold as their unverified canonical triangulations are the same.
          Therefore, we conclude that there are exactly 150,730 isometry classes in the 10-tetrahedra
       census, containing a total of 496,638 minimal triangulations, obtaining Theorem 1.

3.4    Finalizing the census
For each of the 150,730 isometry classes obtained in Section 3.3, we select a representative
triangulation by the following procedure:
(1) If the verified canonical triangulation is in the isometry class, let it be the representative.
(2) Otherwise, consider the subset of triangulations that are geometric, which turns out to
    be never empty. If there is only one triangulation in the class, let it be the representative.
(3) If there are multiple triangulations in that subset, let the triangulation with the most
    self-isomorphisms, i.e. cellular homeomorphisms onto itself, be the representative.
(4) If there are multiple triangulations with the most self-isomorphisms, choose the one
    with the “fattest” tetrahedra, i.e. the one with the largest minimum imaginary part of
    tetrahedron shape parameters.
(5) If there are still multiple options left, choose the one with the smallest triangulation
    signature (as defined in [4]) under the lexicographical order.

   With the representative triangulations chosen as above, we set their peripheral curves
to be the shortest. We then ordered them by volume, named them as displayed in Table 1,
saved and published the data in [34]. The data now comes automatically with SnapPy 3.3.
   Note that verified canonical triangulations, by construction, are always geometric [22].
Hence due to the geometric requirement in step (2), we obtained

▶ Proposition 11. Every cusped hyperbolic 3-manifold in the 10-tetrahedra census admits a
minimal triangulation that is geometric.

We remark that the above proposition also holds for all (orientable) censuses with fewer
tetrahedra, which we checked using Burton’s data from [7].

3.5    Obstructions on further extending the census
As is discussed in Section 3.1, there are essentially three steps for creating a complete
census. For the census of (orientable) cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds, step (ii) should not
be a problem, as there are several other tests proposed in [7], but were not used when
creating the 10-tetrahedra census. For step (iii), the verified computation has a chance of
failing only when the LLL algorithm is invoked, which happens only when a tilt that is
extremely close to zero is encountered during computation. This essentially implies that the
Epstein–Penner cellulation is not a triangulation, which is the case for only 986 triangulations
out of the 608918 orientable candidates mentioned in Section 3.3.3, a frequency less than
0.2%. Therefore, it is promising that a combination of verified canonical triangulations with
algebraic methods would suffice in the foreseeable future, where the former separates most
manifolds, and the latter deals with the rest.
    The main obstruction thus lives in step (i), where an exponential growth rate of the
computational power is needed, with a much larger base compared to tabulating knots [39].
If one were to include nonorientable candidates during generation (as we did in Theorem 7),

         4     Applications
        A substantial amount of follow-up work can be done with the extended census. We describe
        several of them in this section.

        4.1    Extending the census of exceptional Dehn fillings
        Let M be a compact orientable 3-manifold whose interior M is a 1-cusped hyperbolic 3-
        manifold; in particular ∂M is a torus, and M has finite volume. Dehn fillings on M are
        characterized by slopes on ∂M , which are unoriented isotopy classes of simple closed curves
        on the torus. For a slope α, we denote by M (α) the closed manifold obtained by Dehn filling
        on M so that α bounds a disk in the attached solid torus D2 × S 1 .

        ▶ Definition 13. A slope α is exceptional if M (α) is not hyperbolic.

        The census of exceptional Dehn fillings will consist of pairs (M, α), where α is exceptional.
            By deleting a cusp neighborhood N of M , we obtain a compact 3-manifold M \ N with
        torus boundary which is isotopic to M . Slopes on ∂M can thus be carried by the isotopy
        onto ∂(M \ N ) ⊂ M . By taking N to be maximal, we define the length of a slope to be the
        minimum length of all curves in its isotopy class on ∂(M \ N ).
            Agol [1] and Lackenby [31] independently proved that lengths of exceptional slopes cannot
        exceed 6. It follows that there are only finitely many exceptional fillings on a 1-cusped finite-
        volume hyperbolic 3-manifold. Therefore it is possible to give complete lists of exceptional
        Dehn fillings on 1-cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds in the censuses. For censuses of at most 9
        tetrahedra, this has been done by Dunfield [17]. For the 10-tetrahedra census, we obtained:

        ▶ Theorem 14. There are precisely 439,898 exceptional Dehn fillings on orientable 1-cusped
        hyperbolic 3-manifolds in the 10-tetrahedra census.

            Table 3 outlines the procedure for obtaining Theorem 14. There are 144,016 1-cusped
        hyperbolic 3-manifolds in the 10-tetrahedra census. For each of them, we enumerated all
        slopes with length no more than 6, obtaining a total of 800,447 candidates for the exceptional
        census. As no duplicate slopes were enumerated for a given manifold, all candidates are
        distinct, and we only need to decide the hyperbolicity for each of them.
            For each candidate (M, α), we consider its filled manifold M (α). Several rounds of
        certifying the hyperbolicity of M (α) with SnapPy reduced the remaining list by nearly a
        half. For Regina census lookup, we cut M (α) into connected sum summands and used
        regina.Census.lookup to try obtaining a name classifying it, which then tells us whether
        M (α) is hyperbolic or not. For those whose names were not obtained, we check whether they
        have fundamental normal surfaces which are essential S 2 or tori; if they do, they are not
        hyperbolic. Only 11 candidates remain undetermined after this, and their filled manifolds
        were all identified as m135(1,3) by SnapPy. m135(1,3) is isometric to m412(1,-3)(-3,1) whose
        triangulation in SnapPy is certified to be geometric, hence m135(1,3) is hyperbolic.

        4.3    Homology 3-spheres and the L-space conjecture
        The L-space conjecture asserts that for an irreducible Q-homology 3-sphere Y , the following
        are equivalent:
        (a) π1 (Y ) is left-orderable;
        (b) Y has non-minimal Heegaard Floer homology;
        (c) Y admits a taut foliation.
        The equivalence of (a) and (b) was proposed by Boyer, Gordon and Watson [3]. The
        equivalence of (b) and (c) was asked by Ozsváth and Szabó [38] after they proved that
        (c) implies (b), and upgraded to a conjecture by A. Juhász [30]. For Z-homology spheres,
        Calegari and Dunfield [9] proved that (c) implies (a).
             Dunfield [16] showed that the L-space conjecture holds on at least 62.2% of 307,301
        hyperbolic Q-homology 3-spheres, obtained by Dehn fillings on orientable 1-cusped hyperbolic
        3-manifolds in censuses of at most 9 tetrahedra. It was conjectured in [16] that these are
        precisely the filled manifolds from those censuses with lengths of systoles being at least 0.2.
             While there are infinitely many hyperbolic Q-homology 3-spheres obtained by Dehn
        fillings on a finite set of orientable 1-cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds, a finite list is obtained if
        we bound the list by the length of systoles, i.e. the shortest geodesics, from below, as the
        following result was shown by Hodgson and Kerckhoff [26]:

        ▶ Lemma 16 (Hodgson & Kerckhoff). Let M be a compact orientable 3-manifold with torus
        boundary whose interior M is hyperbolic, and α be a slope on ∂M . If M (α) is hyperbolic
        with systole length at least 0.163, then the normalized length of α is no more than 7.515.

        Here, the normalized length of α is the length of α divided by the area of ∂(M \ N ).
             Similarly to Section 4.1, for the 1-cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds in the 10-tetrahedra
        census, by enumerating all slopes with normalized length no more than 7.515, excluding
        all exceptional slopes, and filtering by the length of systole, we obtained a list of 1,899,974
        fillings containing all pairs (M, α) such that M (α) is a hyperbolic Q-homology 3-sphere with
        length of systole at least 0.163. Therefore,

        ▶ Theorem 17. There are precisely 1,899,974 pairs (M, α) where M is a 1-cusped hyperbolic
        3-manifold in the 10-tetrahedra census and α is a slope such that M (α) is a hyperbolic
        Q-homology 3-sphere with length of systole at least 0.163.

        Changing Q to Z in Theorem 17, the number of pairs becomes 10,729.
           Note that, although the pairs (M, α) in Theorem 17 are all distinct, the filled manifolds
        M (α) are not; for instance, there are at least 22 pairs in the list such that M (α) is identical
        to m007(3,1). It remains to group the pairs into distinct isometry classes by M (α), compare
        the grouped list against the list of 307,301 manifolds in [16], and test the L-space conjecture
        on it. We wish to address these in a future publication.

        4.4    Closed totally geodesic surfaces
        An embedded surface S in a hyperbolic 3-manifold M is called totally geodesic if every
        geodesic in S is also a geodesic in M . The existence of closed totally geodesic surfaces is of
        particular interest.
S. Y. Li                                                                                              73:13


    An algorithm that is guaranteed to find all closed totally geodesic surfaces (up to isotopy)
in a given orientable cusped finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifold was built and used to find
several examples of cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds with closed totally geodesic surfaces
by Basilio, Lee and Malionek [2]; however, none was found in the censuses of at most 9
tetrahedra. By applying their algorithm to the 10-tetrahedra census, we found that
▶ Theorem 18. The 2-cusped manifold o10_143602, whose volume is approximately 9.1345
and first homology group is Z2 ⊕ Z6 , is the only manifold containing closed totally geodesic
surfaces in the orientable cusped hyperbolic censuses of at most 10 tetrahedra. Moreover,
o10_143602 contains exactly one such surface up to isotopy, which is nonorientable with
Euler characteristic −1.
In particular, among all orientable cusped hyperbolic 3-manifolds containing closed totally
geodesic surfaces, o10_143602 is the one whose minimal triangulations have the fewest
tetrahedra; in other words, it is the simplest such example.
